findings.label: Vitreous snowballs
findings.evidence: Massive exudates in mid vitreous that block fundoscopic examination of posterior pole

panels.rationale: Single-panel ophthalmic (fundus/vitreal) photograph from an article dedicated to pars planitis. The caption explicitly describes massive mid-vitreous exudates blocking view of the posterior pole, corresponding to the pars planitis vitreous snowball finding in the provided vocabulary; the accompanying in-text discussion identifies such yellow-white mid-vitreous aggregates as a manifestation of pars planitis. No skin is visible, so skin tone and ethnicity are null and the age is not stated for this figure.

findings.label: Cystoid macular edema on OCT
findings.evidence: Late phase of fluorescein angiography showing cystoid macular edema in 11-year-old boy with pars planitis

panels.rationale: Single-panel late-phase fluorescein angiogram of a real pediatric patient with pars planitis, showing the characteristic petaloid cystoid macular edema, a well-recognized manifestation of pars planitis explicitly captioned as such.
panels.attribution_text: Przeździecka-Dołyk et al. Immunopathogenic Background of Pars Planitis.. Archivum immunologiae et therapiae experimentalis 2016. doi:10.1007/s00005-015-0361-y. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Late phase of fluorescein angiography showing cystoid macular edema in 11-year-old boy with pars planitis
in_text_mentions: Cystoid macular edema (CME) was described as a major cause of visual loss (incidence 8–26 %) in patients with pars planitis (Fig. 4). The mean interval between onset of pars planitis and CME was 5.7 years (Babu and Rathinam 2010; Donaldson et al. 2007; Foster and Vitale 2013; Malinowski et al. 1993a; Pruett et al. 1974; Smith et al. 1976). The pathophysiology of cystoid macular edema was described in patients with uveitis without subdividing that group (no data show a pathomechanism of CME in patients with pars planitis). Retinal vascular hyperpermeability can be influenced by several mediator

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Color fundus photograph of a human patient from a pars-planitis-focused article; caption describes disc swelling (optic disc edema, a vocabulary-listed pars planitis sign) with peripapillary subretinal hemorrhage and fluid, which are recorded as proposed findings since they are absent from the vocabulary. b: Optical coherence tomography of the left eye of a human patient showing intraretinal and subretinal fluid temporal to the disc in a pars planitis case with peripapillary choroidal neovascularization (disease-focused article title plus captioned manifestation). The depicted exudative fluid/CNV is not represented in the configured finding vocabulary, so no vocabulary finding is asserted; caption explicitly states no cystoid macular edema. c: Early-phase fluorescein angiogram of a human patient showing a choroidal neovascular membrane adjacent to the disc in the left eye of a pars planitis patient; manifestation is captioned and the...
panels.attribution_text: Mehta et al. Peripapillary choroidal neovascularization in pars planitis.. Journal of ophthalmic inflammation and infection 2013. doi:10.1186/1869-5760-3-13. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Color fundus photograph, optical coherence tomography, and fluorescein angiogram at presentation. (a) Color fundus photograph of the left eye at presentation demonstrating disc swelling with peripapillary subretinal hemorrhage and subretinal fluid. (b) Intraretinal and subretinal fluid temporal to the disc is evident on optical coherence tomography. (c) Early and (d) late fluorescein angiograms of the left eye reveals a choroidal neovascular membrane adjacent to the disc.
in_text_mentions: ronic disc swelling but was otherwise unremarkable. In addition to disc swelling, the left eye fundus showed peripapillary subretinal hemorrhage and subretinal fluid extending into the macula (Figure 1a,b). Fluorescein angiogram showed an active choroidal neovascular membrane adjacent to the disc in the left eye (Figure 1c,d). There was no evidence of cystoid macular edema, periphlebitis, snowballs, or snowbanking in either eye on clinical exam, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and fluorescein angiogram. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Color fundus photograph of the left eye showing vitreous cells, a recognized pars planitis finding; RPE mottling is also noted but not in the vocabulary. B: Fundus photograph of the left eye showing retinal pigmentation that developed three months after onset of bilateral pars planitis, as described in the case report; this is an atypical progression of the disease.
panels.attribution_text: Vela et al. Progression of retinal pigmentation mimicking unilateral retinitis pigmentosa after bilateral pars planitis: a case report.. BMC ophthalmology 2018. doi:10.1186/s12886-018-0814-2. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: a Colour fundus photograph (superior field) of the left eye showing mild RPE mottling, blurred by vitreous cells. Retinal pigment deposits were not observed. b Pigmentation of the retina developed three months after onset
